verified_at: adversarial verification pass for secrets-1 (secrets domain)

finding.title: MASTER_KEY → AES-256 key derivation is a single unsalted SHA-256 round (no KDF iterations); dictionary-strength env passphrase + stolen DB = offline bulk decrypt of every provider API key
finding.evidence: crypto.go:21-23 — `func NewCipher(masterKey string) (*Cipher, error) {` / `sum := sha256.Sum256([]byte(masterKey))` / `block, err := aes.NewCipher(sum[:])`. The env value is accepted verbatim with no minimum length/entropy check (config.go:64 `MasterKey:          getenv("MASTER_KEY", "llm-router-guard-master-key"),`), and every provider key is sealed under this one derived key (providers.go:64 `enc, err := s.enc.Encrypt(req.APIKey)`, stored in providers.api_key_enc, model.go:107).
finding.impact: A single SHA-256 per candidate is GPU-crackable at billions of guesses/sec. If gateway.db (or a MySQL/PG dump) is exfiltrated and the operator chose a human-chosen MASTER_KEY (the code and .env.template encourage copy-paste of the shipped default), all upstream provider API keys (OpenAI/Anthropic billing accounts) are decrypted offline. The warn-only default check (main.go:191-193) fires only for the exact literal default, not for weak-but-custom values — the NEW consequence beyond the stated 'warn-only defaults' fact.
finding.mitigations_checked: AES-GCM itself is correct: 12-byte random nonce per Encrypt call from crypto/rand (crypto.go:34-40), nonce prepended, auth tag verified on Decrypt (crypto.go:52). Ciphertext (not plaintext) is what is stored; nonce-reuse risk negligible at this message volume. No AAD binding to provider ID (ciphertext rows could be swapped between providers inside a stolen DB).
finding.recommendation: Derive the cipher key with a memory-hard iterated KDF (Argon2id or scrypt; PBKDF2-HMAC-SHA256 >=600k iterations as a floor) with a random salt stored alongside the ciphertext header; enforce minimum MASTER_KEY entropy at startup; provide a re-encrypt/rotation tool so MASTER_KEY can actually be changed (today main.go:192 tells operators rotation requires manual re-entry of every provider key).

reason:
VERDICT: downgrade high -> medium. The code claim is 100% accurate and every quote was re-read in place, but the severity as filed overstates the reachability of the weakness: it is a genuine failure of a defense-in-depth control (CWE-916 insufficient key stretching), not a flaw the application's own trust boundary lets anyone exercise. Under this engagement's rubric that is precisely 'medium = defense-in-depth gap with real impact'; it is not 'high = authed-but-severe or account takeover', because the modeled actor is not an application principal at all.

A) EVIDENCE AUDIT — all verbatim, no line corrections needed.
1) crypto.go:21-23 is exactly `func NewCipher(masterKey string) (*Cipher, error) {` / `sum := sha256.Sum256([]byte(masterKey))` / `block, err := aes.NewCipher(sum[:])`. The anchor line 22 is correct as filed (it is the SHA-256 derivation itself), so no corrected_line change.
2) config.go:64 verbatim `MasterKey:          getenv("MASTER_KEY", "llm-router-guard-master-key"),`; getenv (config.go:30-35) returns any non-empty env value untouched, so there is no normalization or floor.
3) providers.go:64 verbatim `enc, err := s.enc.Encrypt(req.APIKey)`; also providers.go:112 for updates.
4) model.go:107 verbatim `APIKeyEnc    string    ` + "`" + `gorm:"type:text" json:"-"` + "`" + ` // AES-GCM 加密存储 (REQ-005 ④)`.
5) main.go:191-193 verbatim `if cfg.MasterKey == "llm-router-guard-master-key" {` and the WARNING on 192 — a case-sensitive single-literal equality test, no entropy/length test, no release-mode refusal, non-blocking.
6) The 'mitigations_checked' text is itself accurate: crypto.go:35-36 draws a fresh `nonce := make([]byte, c.aead.NonceSize())` filled from `io.ReadFull(rand.Reader, nonce)` (12 bytes, cipher.NewGCM default at :27), :39 `ct := c.aead.Seal(nonce, nonce, []byte(plain), nil)` prepends it, :52 `c.aead.Open(nil, raw[:ns], raw[ns:], nil)` enforces the tag. additionalData is nil on both sides, so the 'no AAD binding' note is code-true.

B) THE WEAKNESS IS REAL AND UNMITIGATED IN CODE — this is why it is not refuted.
Whole-repo grep for `MasterKey` yields exactly one producer (config.go:64) and one consumer (main.go:50 `enc, err := crypto.NewCipher(cfg.MasterKey)`). There is no length, charset, or entropy check anywhere between os.Getenv and sha256.Sum256, and none is structurally possible in NewCipher: the SHA-256 digest is always 32 bytes, so `aes.NewCipher(sum[:])` can never reject a weak passphrase and the :24-26 error branch is dead for input-quality purposes. A one-character MASTER_KEY boots silently. Verification of a guessed key is free and unambiguous for the attacker: the AEAD tag at :52 is a zero-false-positive oracle, and the plaintext is short, structured (`sk-proj-...`/`sk-ant-...`), so a candidate is rejected in one SHA-256 + one AES-GCM open. Per-candidate cost is exactly the amount of work an offline cracker wants — no iteration, no memory hardness, and the finding's GPU-throughput claim is sound for single-round SHA-256.

C) BLAST RADIUS, pinned more tightly than filed. The Cipher protects exactly one column: providers.api_key_enc. Encrypt appears only at providers.go:64/112; Decrypt only at providers.go:163 (testProvider), health.go:121 (checker.apiKey), manager.go:214 (runtime reload). Gateway API keys are stored as SHA-256 hashes (apikeys.go:40 `crypto.Sha256Hex(key)`), admin passwords as bcrypt (main.go:175), TOTP recovery codes hashed — none of them derive from MASTER_KEY, and JWT_SECRET is a separate secret. So 'every provider API key' is the whole story, not a subset of a broader key hierarchy; the finding's scope is right but its framing ('bulk decrypt') invites the reader to assume more reaches than it does.

D) EXPOSURE-SURFACE MITIGATIONS THE ORIGINAL AUDITOR DID NOT CHECK — these are what move the needle down. The precondition 'attacker holds the ciphertext' is far harder to satisfy through this application than the title implies:
1) model.go:107 AND :108 (`APIKey       string    ` + "`" + `gorm:"-" json:"-"` + "`" + ` // 运行时内存明文（不入库）`) both carry `json:"-"`, so no handler can serialize ciphertext or the in-memory plaintext. listProviders (providers.go:44 `okPaged(c, rows, ...)`) and create/update responses (providers.go:81-83 and :130 explicitly blank `p.APIKeyEnc = ""` before `s.ok`) expose only api_key_masked. runtime.ResolvedUpstream.APIKey (manager.go:244-246) is an internal-only struct never marshaled by any route (grep: it appears only in runtime, slb, gateway and tests).
2) The operator's own backup/export artifacts contain NO crackable material: ConfigBundle.Providers is []model.Provider (bundle.go:17) so exportConfig (configstatus.go:68 `body, _ := json.MarshalIndent(b, ...)`) and createBackup (backup.go:31 `body, _ := json.Marshal(b)`, stored in backup_records.Content and served by downloadBackup at :53) emit providers with the key fields stripped. The bundle.go:15 comment ('密钥保持 DB 原样密文') is in fact wrong — the ciphertext is silently dropped — which is a functional/restore defect in another domain, but here it is a real mitigation: the most commonly leaked artifact class in self-hosted deployments (config.json / backup-*.json emailed to support) is not a source of ciphertext.
3) Operation logs likewise cannot carry it: recordOp (server.go:94-96) -> audit.LogOp (audit.go:110-119) serializes before/after with json.Marshal, so the `p`/`before` snapshots passed at providers.go:79/:128 omit APIKeyEnc too.
4) There is no online oracle: Decrypt is called only on stored values, and every failure path is swallowed (providers.go:163 `key, _ := s.enc.Decrypt(...)`, health.go:122-124 `return ""`, manager.go:218 `p.APIKey = ""`). No request path lets a client submit candidate key material or observe distinguishable decrypt errors, so the attack cannot be run against the live service.
Net: the ONLY way to obtain the input to the cracking job is a direct read of providers.api_key_enc in the storage engine — the SQLite file itself, or a MySQL/PG dump/replica. That is an out-of-band breach the application does not cause. And in the default single-node topology the breach that yields gateway.db almost always yields the process environment (or the very .env the compose file auto-reads) as well, in which case the attacker reads MASTER_KEY instead of cracking it. The KDF gap bites only in the narrower 'DB-only exposure' case (leaked SQL dump, read-only replica, object-storage snapshot, table-scoped injection) — real, but conditional.

E) THE 'ALREADY HAS THE PRIVILEGE' TEST, applied honestly. In the multi-node MySQL/PG topology the DB-only-exposure case is exactly the scenario at-rest encryption exists for, and there the finding holds: the weak derivation is the only thing standing between a leaked dump and every OpenAI/Anthropic billing key. That is why this is medium with real impact and not 'low/hygiene'. Conversely, an attacker with DB *write* access does not need this weakness at all (they can insert their own provider row or repoint an alias upstream and capture keys live), which is also why the 'no AAD binding, rows could be swapped' note adds zero severity — flagged below as a correction, not a refutation.

F) NOT MERELY A RE-REPORT OF THE PRE-AGREED 'warn-only defaults' FACT. The stated architecture fact covers the *default value*; this finding covers what happens *after* an operator sets a custom value — the result is still a single unsalted SHA-256 with no entropy floor (B above). That is a distinct defect and it survives the instruction. One claim in the impact paragraph does need correcting: '.env.template encourage[s] copy-paste of the shipped default' is overstated — .env.template:3 says `cp .env.template .env && 编辑 .env`, :19 says `# ---- 密钥（生产环境必须替换！默认值启动时会打印 [security] WARNING）----`, README.md:143 shows `MASTER_KEY="your-strong-secret"`, quickstart.md:52/90 repeat it, and help.ts:47/51 surface it in the console UI. Documentation warns loudly; only enforcement is missing. The genuinely un-warned weak value is docker-compose.yml:16 `- MASTER_KEY=${MASTER_KEY:-CHANGE-ME-MASTER-KEY}`, which (a) is itself dictionary-strength and (b) never equals main.go:191's lowercase literal, so a container started with no .env runs a weak-but-custom master key with zero log output. That strengthens the impact story — but it is already carried by authn-1's sibling (verify-authn-1-2, per docs/security/raw/verify-authn-1.json), so counting it a second time here must not inflate this finding's severity.

G) TECHNICAL CORRECTIONS TO THE WRITE-UP (verdict-neutral). (1) 'unsalted' is a mislabeled axis: with one global master key mandated identical across every instance (README.md:263 'MASTER_KEY … 所有实例必须完全一致'), a per-record salt buys nothing against an offline dictionary attack on that single secret; the missing property is stretching (iteration/memory-hardness), and the recommendation's 'random salt stored alongside the ciphertext header' also implies a storage-format change plus a per-instance salt-provenance problem the finding does not address. (2) 'nonce-reuse risk negligible at this message volume' is right but under-argued: the nonce is fresh from crypto/rand on every Encrypt (:35-36), so reuse is a 2^-bound birthday event, not a volume heuristic. (3) Minor aggravator the finding missed: MaskKey (crypto.go:65 `return string(r[:4]) + "****" + string(r[len(r)-2:])`) is persisted in api_key_masked and shipped in every provider listing/export/backup, handing the cracker a known 4+2-char prefix/suffix and the exact plaintext length per row — a marginal speedup, not a new boundary. (4) Rotation: grep finds no re-seal path anywhere in internal/admin, so main.go:192 and help.ts:51 ('变更后历史密文无法解密') are accurate — an unusable-in-practice key is a legitimate part of this medium, and the rotation-tool recommendation stands.

H) SEVERITY MAPPING (final). Unauth RCE / authz bypass / data exfil -> no: nothing network-facing accepts input that reaches the cryptosystem, and no app surface returns ciphertext. Authed-but-severe / account takeover -> no: an authenticated admin gains nothing from the weakness (D1-D3) and does not need it (E). Defense-in-depth gap with real impact -> yes, exactly: an at-rest encryption control that is implemented but not key-stretched, so its security degrades to the entropy of one env var, with high-value secrets (all upstream billing keys) behind it, no entropy floor, no rotation path, and one shipped deployment path (compose fallback) that suppresses even the warning. medium, corrected_line 22 unchanged.
exploit_sketch:
Preconditions: (i) the attacker has obtained providers.api_key_enc rows out of band — the SQLite file gateway.db, or a MySQL/PostgreSQL dump/replica/object-storage snapshot (NOT via the app: model.go:107/108 are json:"-", so /api/admin/v1/providers, /config/export and /backups/:id/download all omit ciphertext and plaintext entirely; and there is no online decrypt oracle — Decrypt is called only on stored values with errors swallowed at providers.go:163, health.go:122, manager.go:218); and (ii) the operator's MASTER_KEY has low guessing entropy. Nothing in the code enforces (ii): config.go:64 passes the env value straight to main.go:50 -> crypto.go:22 `sha256.Sum256([]byte(masterKey))`, so the derived key is exactly as strong as the passphrase.

Offline bulk-recovery job (single-round SHA-256 per candidate, no stretching):

  # candidate list: the shipped values themselves are candidates
  printf '%s\n' llm-router-guard-master-key CHANGE-ME-MASTER-KEY e2e-master-key-2026 \
    $(cat rockyou.txt) > cands.txt

  # one candidate -> one AES-256 key, exactly as crypto.go:22 does
  key=$(printf '%s' "$CAND" | sha256sum | cut -c1-64)

  # row format is base64(nonce[12] || ciphertext || tag[16])  (crypto.go:39-40)
  python3 - <<'EOF'
  import base64, sys
  from hashlib import sha256
  from cryptography.hazmat.primitives.ciphers.aead import AESGCM
  enc = open('row.b64').read().strip()          # providers.api_key_enc
  cand = sys.argv[1].encode()                   # candidate MASTER_KEY
  raw = base64.b64decode(enc)
  try:
      pt = AESGCM(sha256(cand).digest()).open(raw[:12], raw[12:], None)
      print('HIT', pt.decode())                 # GCM tag = zero-false-positive oracle
  except Exception:
      pass                                      # wrong key
  EOF

Cost per candidate is one SHA-256 + one AES-GCM open on a ~40-110 byte buffer, verifiable with no ambiguity; api_key_masked (crypto.go:65 -> first 4 + last 2 chars, plus the row's exact plaintext length) narrows each check further. A dictionary-strength passphrase (or either shipped placeholder) falls in seconds-to-minutes on GPU, and once it falls the same key decrypts EVERY provider row in the dump at once — one key for the whole table, no per-row isolation. The realistic delivery of the dump is the multi-node MySQL/PG topology (DB_DSN pointing at an external engine; README.md:263 mandates one shared MASTER_KEY for all instances), i.e. the leak where the app's own encryption-at-rest control is supposed to hold and, unlike an AES key from a real KDF, does not.

What is NOT possible via this weakness, and why severity is medium rather than high: no authentication bypass (JWT_SECRET is independent), no access to gateway API keys (SHA-256 hashes, apikeys.go:40), no access to admin password hashes (bcrypt, main.go:175), and no code path in which an untrusted value is ever used as or compared against the master key. An attacker with host-level access (the usual way gateway.db is taken in the default single-node deployment) reads MASTER_KEY from the environment/.env instead of cracking it; an attacker with admin UI access does not need the key at all (they re-enter keys via createProvider). The impact therefore realizes only in the DB-read-only-leak x weak-passphrase intersection — real, valuable, but two independent conditions outside the application's own boundary.
